units.title: Unit 53 — Talking about cause and effect
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 110–111 (PDF pages 114–115).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose an appropriate verb to describe a causal relationship and distinguish reactions from outcomes.
Contrast immediate and underlying causes and describe the magnitude and direction of consequences.
Use impact, result, effect, outcome and influence with their natural lexical partners.
Distinguish the verb affect, the formal verb effect and the noun effect in context.

items.example: A sudden network failure could cause chaos across the company.
items.note: Cause commonly combines with severe disruption or other negative outcomes.

items.example: The flooding caused havoc in several coastal towns.
items.note: Havoc suggests widespread disruption or destruction and often follows cause.

items.pt: causar muitos danos; provocar grandes estragos
items.example: A voltage surge could cause a lot of damage to sensitive laboratory equipment.
items.note: Damage is normally uncountable in this meaning; use a lot of rather than many damages.

items.example: The unexpected test result caused alarm among the researchers.
items.note: Alarm describes an anxious or fearful reaction, not a physical alarm device.

items.example: The repeated delays caused concern among the project sponsors.
items.note: A conventional way to express that a situation worries people.

items.pt: provocar muita ansiedade; causar grande apreensão
items.example: Uncertainty about the company’s future caused great anxiety among staff.
items.note: Anxiety is usually uncountable; great intensifies the emotional effect.

items.example: The mistaken announcement caused embarrassment for the organisers.
items.note: Use cause with embarrassment when an event makes someone feel ashamed or awkward.

items.pt: provocar uma revolução; desencadear uma grande transformação
items.example: The new manufacturing process could bring about a revolution in battery design.
items.note: Bring about means cause a significant change, often through a process.

items.example: Better public transport could bring about a transformation in the city centre.
items.note: Usually indicates a major or fundamental change, whether good or bad.

items.example: Several scandals helped bring about the downfall of the administration.
items.note: Downfall refers to the loss of power, status or success.

items.pt: provocar o colapso de; causar a derrocada de
items.example: The withdrawal of funding could bring about the collapse of the scheme.
items.note: Often used of governments, organisations, systems or other large structures.

items.pt: conscientizar sobre; gerar conhecimento a respeito de
items.example: The campaign aims to create awareness of online fraud.
items.note: Awareness refers to people recognising or understanding an issue; raise awareness is also common.

items.example: Changing the requirements at the last minute may create problems for the team.
items.note: Create can describe causing new situations, including difficulties.

items.example: The disputed decision could spark off riots in the capital.
items.note: Spark off suggests an event immediately triggers a larger reaction.

items.example: The policy announcement sparked off demonstrations across the region.
items.note: Often used for protests set in motion by a particular incident.

items.pt: dar origem a boatos; desencadear rumores
items.example: The manager’s sudden departure sparked off rumours about a takeover.
items.note: Spark off can introduce unverified speculation as well as public events.

items.example: The proposal attracted criticism for its lack of detail.
items.note: Attract describes the response something receives; criticism is usually uncountable.

items.example: The prototype attracted interest from several overseas partners.
items.note: Often used when a product, idea, person or event draws attention.

items.example: The charity project attracted support from local businesses.
items.note: Support is normally uncountable and can come from individuals or organisations.

items.example: The strict rules may produce the opposite effect and discourage participation.
items.note: Used when the result is contrary to what someone hoped or intended.

items.example: The new approach may take several months to produce results.
items.note: Produce is natural with results in research, interventions and other processes.

items.example: The engineers identified the immediate cause of the shutdown within an hour.
items.note: The immediate cause is the direct event that triggered a problem.

items.pt: a causa subjacente; a causa fundamental
items.example: The investigation revealed that poor maintenance was the underlying cause of the fault.
items.note: Underlying refers to a deeper contributing reason rather than the first visible trigger.

items.example: Additional insulation should reduce the impact of outside noise.
items.note: Reduce the impact means lessen how strongly something affects people or things.

items.example: We scheduled the upgrade overnight to minimise the impact on users.
items.note: Minimise means make as small as reasonably possible; British spelling is minimise.

items.pt: ampliar o impacto; reforçar o efeito
items.example: Clear visual evidence can strengthen the impact of a presentation.
items.note: Strengthen emphasises making an existing effect more powerful.

items.example: Public workshops helped increase the impact of the research project.
items.note: Increase expresses a larger effect or influence; it need not be negative.

items.example: The trial had an unexpected outcome that changed our priorities.
items.note: Outcome is a result of an action or process; unexpected says it was not anticipated.

items.example: The reform may have an unforeseen outcome for smaller companies.
items.note: Unforeseen means not predicted or considered in advance.

items.example: Long queues were a predictable outcome of the reduced train service.
items.note: Predictable indicates that the result could reasonably be expected.

items.example: Without new investment, further delays seem an inevitable outcome.
items.note: Inevitable suggests that an outcome cannot realistically be avoided.

items.example: The training programme had positive effects on staff confidence.
items.note: Effects refers to the consequences of an action or event; positive evaluates them favourably.

items.example: Regular breaks can have beneficial effects on concentration.
items.note: Beneficial stresses that the effects help or improve a situation.

items.example: The report describes the negative effects of prolonged noise exposure.
items.note: Negative effects means unfavourable consequences; adverse is a more formal alternative.

items.example: The medication may have adverse effects in some patients.
items.note: Adverse is often formal or technical, especially for unwanted consequences.

items.pt: uma consequência direta; um resultado direto
items.example: The power cut was a direct result of damaged cables.
items.note: Direct indicates a close causal link without significant intermediate steps.

items.pt: um resultado inevitável; uma consequência inevitável
items.example: Higher maintenance costs were an inevitable result of the ageing machinery.
items.note: Inevitable describes a result that was virtually certain to happen.

items.pt: um resultado indireto; uma consequência indireta
items.example: New jobs were an indirect result of investment in the railway.
items.note: An indirect result comes about through additional steps or secondary effects.

items.example: One unforeseen result of the new timetable was increased weekend traffic.
items.note: Unforeseen describes an effect that planners did not anticipate.

items.pt: causar grande polêmica; provocar uma onda de protestos
items.example: The decision to close the library caused an uproar in the neighbourhood.
items.note: Uproar describes strong and often noisy public anger or protest.

items.example: If you ignore the safety procedures, you may suffer the consequences.
items.note: Suggests bearing negative results, often of one’s own actions.

items.example: The redesign had a huge effect on the machine’s reliability.
items.note: Have an effect on is the standard construction for influence or change.

items.example: The discovery could have a major impact on renewable energy.
items.note: Impact usually takes on before the affected person, activity or area.

items.example: Interrupting every speaker can make a bad impression at an interview.
items.note: Use make an impression, not do an impression, for the effect on other people.

items.example: Being prepared helps create a good impression on new colleagues.
items.note: Create and make both combine with impression in this sense.

items.word: have a lot of influence on
items.example: Online reviews have a lot of influence on consumer choices.
items.note: Influence on names the people or decisions affected; influence is uncountable here.

items.example: The unexpected performance caused a sensation at the festival.
items.note: Describes an event attracting widespread excitement or public attention.

items.example: An unexpected loss can affect people deeply for a long time.
items.note: Affect is a verb meaning influence; here deeply describes emotional strength.

items.pt: efetuar uma mudança; promover uma mudança
items.example: The organisation hopes to effect a change in how services are delivered.
items.note: Formal effect is a verb meaning bring about; do not confuse it with affect, meaning influence.

items.example: The new lighting had an effect on how accurately we could inspect the parts.
items.note: Effect here is a noun, unlike the verbs affect and effect.

items.example: The mentor had a considerable influence on my career plans.
items.note: Considerable expresses a substantial degree of influence.

items.example: Poor access to schooling can affect development in many ways.
items.note: Affect takes a direct object; do not add on after this verb.

items.example: A clear summary can strengthen the impact of the findings.
items.note: A variant of strengthen the impact that names the source of the influence.

items.example: Experienced colleagues can exert an influence on workplace culture.
items.note: A more formal verb–noun combination; listed as a possible dictionary extension in the key.

items.example: The team will assess the effect of the update after a week.
items.note: Assess means evaluate how significant or beneficial an effect is; offered as dictionary-study material.

items.example: The shortcut could have adverse consequences for data security.
items.note: Consequences can be harmful; adverse is a formal adjective used with negative outcomes.

sectionsChecked: A · Different cause verbs: cause, bring about, create, spark off, attract and produce
B · Causes and effects: immediate/underlying causes, impact, outcome, effects and results
C · Common expressions for everyday events and affect/effect contrast

units.title: Unit 54 — Remembering and sensing
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 112–113 (PDF pages 116–117).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe long-term and short-term memory, degrees of recollection and forgotten details.
Use figurative memory expressions such as go blank, come flooding back, stir up and blot out.
Express uncertain perceptions using impression, feeling, sense and intuition.
Distinguish physical sensitivity and sharp senses from sensible judgement and emotional sensitivity.

items.example: Long-term memory allows us to recall things learned years ago.
items.note: Refers to the retention of information and experiences over long periods.

items.example: Stress can make it harder to use your short-term memory effectively.
items.note: Refers to information retained briefly; contrast long-term memory.

items.example: She has a good memory for names and faces.
items.note: The normal construction is have a good memory, not make a good memory in this sense.

items.example: I cannot remember his surname, so give me a clue.
items.note: An informal request for a hint to help recall or guess something.

items.example: That melody reminds me strongly of the music my grandparents played.
items.note: Remind someone of links a present thing to a person or memory; strongly adds intensity.

items.example: I vaguely remember visiting that museum as a child.
items.note: Vaguely means without clear or complete details; distinctly contrasts with it.

items.example: I had clean forgotten about the appointment until you called.
items.note: Clean is an informal intensifier with forgotten, especially in British English.

items.example: By the next morning, I had completely forgotten the password.
items.note: Completely is a neutral alternative to informal clean with forgotten.

items.pt: me deu um branco; minha mente ficou em branco
items.example: My mind went blank when the interviewer asked an unexpected question.
items.note: Describes temporarily being unable to remember or think clearly.

items.example: I can remember a face for years but often forget the person’s name.
items.note: An example of remembering recognition information rather than a name.

items.pt: as lembranças vêm à tona de uma vez
items.example: Old memories come flooding back whenever I hear that song.
items.note: Flooding back means returning suddenly and in large numbers.

items.example: My earliest memory is of playing in my grandmother’s garden.
items.note: Earliest refers to the first experience a person can recall.

items.pt: despertar lembranças; trazer lembranças à tona
items.example: Looking through the old photographs can stir up memories of our school days.
items.note: Stir up suggests prompting memories, sometimes difficult or emotional ones.

items.example: I distinctly remember locking the office door before leaving.
items.note: Distinctly signals a clear, specific recollection; compare vaguely remember.

items.pt: apagar uma lembrança; tentar esquecer uma lembrança
items.example: He wished he could blot out a memory of the frightening accident.
items.note: A figurative expression for trying to suppress a disturbing memory.

items.example: I vividly remember the excitement of my first flight.
items.note: Vividly emphasises how strongly and clearly the experience is recalled.

items.example: Watching the northern lights was an unforgettable experience.
items.note: Describes an experience so striking that it is likely to be remembered.

items.example: If I remember rightly, we met at a conference in 2022.
items.note: Used to qualify a recollection politely when not completely certain.

items.example: I remember well how nervous I felt on my first day.
items.note: Well describes the clarity or strength of a recollection.

items.pt: as lembranças se apagam; as memórias vão perdendo a nitidez
items.example: Even important memories fade as the years go by.
items.note: Fade means become gradually less clear or detailed.

items.example: The photograph brought back painful memories of that difficult period.
items.note: Painful is emotional rather than physical in this memory collocation.

items.pt: uma experiência marcante; uma experiência memorável
items.example: The visit to the observatory was a memorable experience for the students.
items.note: Memorable usually expresses something remarkable or worth remembering.

items.example: I have the impression that we have already discussed this problem.
items.note: Have the impression introduces a personal judgement that may be uncertain.

items.example: I got the impression that the client was pleased with the demonstration.
items.note: Get suggests forming an impression; have describes holding it.

items.pt: perceber tensão; sentir um clima tenso
items.example: I could sense tension in the room before the vote.
items.note: Sense refers to recognising something without necessarily being told directly.

items.pt: ter a sensação; ter um pressentimento
items.example: I have a feeling that the meeting will take longer than expected.
items.note: Used for an intuition or impression without clear proof.

items.example: I usually trust my intuition when something about an offer seems wrong.
items.note: Trust intuition means rely on instinctive judgement rather than explicit evidence.

items.example: He accused me of being ridiculously over-sensitive about the joke.
items.note: Over-sensitive means reacting too strongly to perceived criticism; ridiculously is emphatic.

items.example: This material is sensitive to heat and must be stored carefully.
items.note: Sensitive to names a stimulus that produces a strong reaction.

items.example: Some electronic sensors are extremely sensitive to light.
items.note: Sensitive to can describe physical responsiveness, not just emotions.

items.example: She uses a mild soap because she has sensitive skin.
items.note: Sensitive describes skin that reacts easily to products or conditions.

items.example: He switched toothpaste because he had sensitive teeth.
items.note: A common term for teeth that react painfully to hot, cold or sweet substances.

items.example: My fingers go numb when I cycle without gloves in winter.
items.note: Go indicates a change of state; numb means without normal physical feeling.

items.example: Dogs often have an acute sense of smell.
items.note: Acute means exceptionally sharp or well developed in reference to a sense.

items.example: The wildlife guide relied on her acute hearing to locate the birds.
items.note: Acute with hearing means unusually sensitive, not sudden or severe.

items.pt: uma pessoa sensível; uma pessoa que se magoa facilmente
items.example: He is a sensitive person who takes critical remarks to heart.
items.note: Sensitive can mean easily hurt emotionally; contrast sensible.

items.pt: uma pessoa sensata; uma pessoa prudente
items.example: A sensible person would check the instructions before operating the machine.
items.note: Sensible means showing sound judgement, not easily upset.

items.example: When you notice warning signs, trust your intuition and investigate further.
items.note: Your is a normal possessive alternative to my in this expression.

sectionsChecked: A · Remembering: remembering, forgetting and recalling
B · Sensing: intuition, impressions, sensitivity and perception
